column4: The accidental killing rule explicitly requires وَدِيَةٌ مُسَلَّمَةٌ إِلَى أَهْلِهِ, the section's exact secondary sense of the w-d-y root: blood money delivered to the victim's family.
This is the core family blood-claim scene: retaliation is prescribed for the slain, a surviving “brother” may remit, and fair payment must then be made to him.
The statement that retaliation contains life gives the section's “my life” its precise legal echo, while the address to people of understanding parallels 89:5's appeal to one possessing discernment.
The guardian of one wrongfully killed receives authority, but may not exceed the limit in killing; it both stages the section's bereaved claimant and confines blood vengeance.
وَلَن يَتِرَكُمْ أَعْمَالَكُمْ uses the section's w-t-r root in its “diminish a right” sense and promises that God will subtract nothing from the believers' deeds.
The deniers demand evil before good although ٱلْمَثُلَاتُ, exemplary punishments, have already passed before them; this is the exact punitive sense developed from 89:8.
إِنَّ جَهَنَّمَ كَانَتْ مِرْصَادًا repeats the watchpost noun and makes Hell itself the waiting station of recompense.
When the first witnesses prove untrustworthy, two nearer lawful claimants take their place and swear; this closely parallels a grave right being pursued through oaths allocated to kin.
At the approach of death, two witnesses are detained and made to swear by God; 5:107 then transfers that oath-bearing role to the nearer claimants if betrayal appears.
The threat of counter-oaths after the first oaths is said to discipline testimony, completing 5:106–107's legal scene of death, claimants, and distributed swearing.
“Life for life” and like-for-like retaliation state the measured blood claim, while remission as charity marks the merciful boundary to exact repayment.
An injury may be repaid only with its like, but pardon and reconciliation move the claimant's reward to God; this directly illuminates measured vengeance and a recompense kept by the Lord.
The punished Sabbath-breakers are made a deterrent example for those around and after them, precisely the section's sense of a penalty made exemplary so others recoil.
The thief's penalty is called both recompense for what was earned and a deterrent from God, joining the section's exemplary punishment to exact requital.
God seizes Pharaoh with an exemplary punishment for his latter and former offense, making the section's named tyrant a deterrent instance.
The verse declares Pharaoh's fate in 79:25 a lesson for whoever fears, explicitly turning punishment into the warning-example perceived by a receptive hearer.
When Pharaoh's people provoke God, He takes vengeance and drowns them all; divine requital produces the example named in the next ayah.
God makes Pharaoh's people a precedent and “an example for the later ones,” the clearest parallel to the section's past peoples preserved as deterrent punishments.
A single catalogue joins Noah's people, ʿĀd, and Pharaoh “of the stakes”; 38:13 adds Thamud and 38:14 states that punishment became due.
Thamud is added to the same exemplary roll as ʿĀd and Pharaoh in 38:12, preparing 38:14's common verdict.
Each listed people denied the messengers, so God's punishment came due; the ayah supplies the shared requital that makes 38:12–13's nations examples.
Deliberate murder is followed by Hell, divine anger, curse, and a tremendous punishment, moving an earthly blood crime into the Lord's final requital.
The first brother's soul induces him to kill his brother, providing the Quran's stark family-murder scene behind the section's implied slain person and bereaved kin.
The decree following that fratricide equates unjustly killing one soul with killing all people and saving one with saving all, giving the life-preserving boundary behind retaliation.
A slain person and the community's dispute over the killing directly stage the concealed homicide and contested right that the section's family oaths seek to resolve.
God exposes the murder of 2:72 by bringing the victim to life, so the hidden blood claim is answered by divine disclosure and a sign of resurrection.
On Judgment Day the murdered girl herself is summoned as the claimant; 81:9 voices the question that ensures her otherwise hidden blood is not lost.
“For what sin was she killed?” makes an unavenged victim's case present before God, where the section's final requital exceeds what any human guardian supplied.
God will not diminish anything from the believers' deeds, restating without w-t-r the precise assurance expressed by 47:35 and the section's claim that requital is not lost.
God joins believing descendants to their family and diminishes nothing from their work, combining the family image with the preservation of every earned right.
God answers that He never lets any worker's work be lost, mentions men and women as “one from another,” and promises those killed a preserved reward.
The record omits neither small nor great and people find their deeds present; this makes concrete the section's claim that recompense stays in place until account.
Just scales are set, no soul is wronged, and even a mustard-seed weight is brought forth, portraying exact requital held until the final reckoning.
Whoever does an atom's weight of good will see it, a concise statement that beneficence remains available for repayment.
Whoever does an atom's weight of evil will see it, extending the watchpost image from preserved reward to unavoidable penalty.
“Is the recompense of excellence anything but excellence?” directly matches the dictionary explanation of keeping another's good until it can be repaid.
God is not heedless of wrongdoers but only delays them to a fixed day, the temporal posture of a Lord stationed in wait for account.
God never breaks His promise to the messengers and is possessor of vengeance; after 14:42's delay, requital is certain rather than forgotten.
The watchpost of 78:21 is specifically a destination for transgressors, identifying whom the waiting station receives.
The punishment at the watchpost is “a fitting recompense,” stating the measured payment that 78:21's scene holds ready.
The reason given is that they did not expect an account, making explicit the reckoning that the section says the watcher awaits.
God places a guard before and behind a chosen messenger; this uses r-s-d for literal watchers whose purpose is explained through encompassing knowledge and counting in 72:28.
God encompasses the messengers and counts everything exactly, completing 72:27's r-s-d guard scene with the account-like enumeration sensed in the section's watchpost.
The divine speaker swears by the settings of the stars, introducing the explicitly named qasam of 56:76.
The oath is called a tremendous قَسَم “if you knew,” closely paralleling 89:5's question whether its oath is sufficient for a discerning mind.
After the opening oaths, the speaker declares the promised event true; 51:6 identifies that promise as certain requital.
The oath sequence culminates in “the recompense will surely occur,” matching this section's movement from oath to a Lord holding payment ready.
A sequence of oaths culminates in the certainty of the Lord's punishment, reproducing the section's structural passage from sworn signs to requital.
“No one can avert it” gives 52:7's divine punishment the unmatched finality heard beside 89:25.
God inflicts “the greatest punishment” on the one who turns away, a close parallel to the final penalty no human avenger can perform.
The return of all people is to God, locating the unmatched punishment of 88:24 in the divine rather than familial forum.
Their account belongs to God, completing 88:24–25 with the reckoning awaited at the section's watchpost.
Salih asks Thamud why they hasten evil before good, almost exactly restaging 13:6's demand for punishment before mercy within one of the section's named peoples.
God tells the reader to see the outcome of Thamud's plot: He destroys them and their people, turning their scheme into visible requital.
Their houses lie ruined for their wrongdoing and are declared a sign for people who know, explicitly making 27:51's punishment exemplary.
The believing man in Pharaoh's house warns of a fate “like” that of Noah's people, ʿĀd, and Thamud, using earlier destroyed peoples to deter Pharaoh from injustice.
The stories of earlier peoples contain a lesson for people of understanding, joining exemplary history to the discerning addressee invoked by the section's oath.
After an unexpected communal punishment, the hearers are commanded to take warning, explicitly turning a historical downfall into an example for perceptive people.
If people retaliate, they may do so only to the measure inflicted on them, while patience is better; this is the exact limit that keeps a blood claim from excess.
One who answers injury with its equal and is then attacked is promised God's help, combining measured retaliation with the Lord's ultimate redress.
The rule to answer aggression only in equal measure supplies another explicit Quranic boundary against the escalation natural to blood vengeance.
An evil deed receives only its like, while righteous good receives provision without measure; exact liability and overflowing grace distinguish two forms of divine repayment.
A good deed is multiplied tenfold while an evil deed is repaid only with its equivalent and no one is wronged, clarifying both preservation and the merciful asymmetry of requital.
No bearer carries another's burden; this individual-liability rule opposes any clan feud that would make a relative answer for the killer's blood debt.
Hatred of a people may not drive believers away from justice, a direct ethical curb on the animus surrounding vengeance for slain kin.
The threatened brother refuses to stretch out his hand to kill even if attacked, a deliberate refusal of reciprocal bloodshed before the fratricide in 5:30.
Moses objects to killing a pure soul “not in retaliation for a soul,” stating the life-for-life boundary precisely by protesting its apparent breach.
A building is prepared as an irṣād, an outpost for one who fought God and His messenger; this corrupt human station reverses the Lord's just watchpost of recompense.
A husband with no witnesses in a grave family accusation supplies four sworn attestations himself; it is a close legal analogue to using apportioned oaths when ordinary proof is absent.
The husband's fifth invocation places God's curse on him if he lies, giving the oath procedure an explicitly deferred divine sanction.
The wife averts the legal punishment through four counter-attestations by God, so opposed family claims are bounded by balanced oath-taking rather than private violence.
Her fifth invocation places God's wrath on her if the husband is truthful, returning the unresolved family claim to divine recompense.
“Lie in wait for them at every marṣad” preserves the literal human ambush behind the section's metaphor of a watcher stationed for what will come.
An eavesdropper finds a flame lying in wait, a supernatural r-s-d ambush that supplies the spatial sense of the section's divine watchpost.
Every utterance meets an observer standing ready, a concrete account scene in which nothing passes the waiting watcher unrecorded.
No deed and not even an atom's weight escapes the Lord, and all is in a clear record; this specifies how held recompense cannot disappear.
Even a mustard-seed weight hidden in rock, heaven, or earth is brought forth by God, making the “not lost” claim spatially vivid.
God does not let the reward of anyone who does good work be lost, a direct nonlexical equivalent of keeping beneficence until repayment.
Every valley the believers cross is written for them so God may reward them; the literal wādī unexpectedly meets the section's separate motif of recompense kept on record.
One who kills game intentionally owes an equivalent judged by two just persons, joining killing, the m-th-l sense of equivalence, and measured compensation in a different legal domain.
Before the fratricide, the threatened brother assigns the killer's burden to him and names the Fire as his requital, anticipating the human killing and divine payment in 5:30.
The raven teaches the killer how to cover his brother's corpse and he becomes remorseful, supplying the bodily aftermath of the Quran's archetypal family murder.
Moses strikes a man and unintentionally causes his death, a narrative instance against which 4:92's accidental-killing compensation can be understood.
Moses immediately confesses wrong and receives forgiveness, showing divine pardon in the accidental killing scene while 4:92 states the surviving family's earthly due.
God presents a secure, well-provided town as an example and then clothes it in hunger and fear for ingratitude, making communal punishment into a warning image.
The audience lived in the dwellings of earlier wrongdoers, saw how God dealt with them, and received examples; past punishment is made present as deterrence.
ʿĀd and Thamud are recalled through dwellings still visible to the hearers, so their destroyed societies remain concrete warning-examples.
Each earlier people is seized for its sin by wind-borne stones, blast, earth-collapse, or drowning; the varied penalties complete 29:38's exemplary catalogue.
Thamud and ʿĀd jointly deny the overwhelming judgment, opening another compact catalogue of the section's warning-peoples.
Thamud is destroyed by the overwhelming blast, giving the first specific exemplary penalty in the catalogue.
ʿĀd is destroyed by a furious wind, placing its distinct requital beside Thamud's.
Pharaoh and the overturned towns are added to the same sequence of peoples who brought grave offenses.
Their disobedience is answered by a surpassing seizure, stating the recompense common to 69:4–9's examples.
The preserved ark is made a reminder received by an attentive ear, explicitly stating why scenes of past punishment and rescue are kept before later hearers.
Thamud denies Salih, kills the she-camel, and is crushed by the Lord for its sin, another direct instance of the named people becoming exemplary punishment.
God does not fear the consequence of leveling Thamud, underscoring how divine requital exceeds the constraints and vulnerability of a human avenger.
The hearer is asked whether the story of the hosts has reached him, introducing Pharaoh and Thamud as remembered warning forces.
Pharaoh and Thamud are named together as the hosts whose story 85:17 invokes, repeating two of the section's exemplary peoples.
God encompasses the deniers from behind, a spatial parallel to the watchpost's inescapable oversight after the Pharaoh-and-Thamud reminder.
Precedents have passed before the hearers, who are told to travel and inspect the deniers' end; earlier punishment is offered for present deterrence.
The hearers are told to inspect the end of earlier peoples whom God destroyed, with “the like of it” awaiting disbelievers; exemplary past and promised counterpart meet.
After a chain of divine oaths, the promised event is declared inevitable, a structural parallel to this section's oath leading toward stored requital.
On the day of the greatest seizure God declares “We will take vengeance,” locating the final blood-debt vocabulary in divine judgment.

The brothers bring false blood on Joseph's shirt to persuade their father that a family member was killed; it is a specific inversion of a true blood claim, though no homicide or lawful oath occurred.
